components.text: This course introduces students to rhetorical concepts and audience-centered approaches to writing including composing processes, language conventions and style, and critical analysis and engagement with written texts and other forms of communication.

components.title: Course Requisites

components.text: Discussion-based and collaborative course engagement are significant means of learning in this course. Modality is either in-person or asynchronous online, and full engagement in course learning is heavily emphasized in both modalities. Students are expected to read, discuss, interact, participate, reflect, draft and revise, respond to feedback, and otherwise engage as instructed in a sequenced set of assignments that lead to completion of each of four projects. Projects are scaffolded to build learning throughout the course, and require engagement in the writing processes and learning activities in order to meet student learning outcomes.
components.title: Course Format

components.text:
Students will apply rhetorical knowledge to communicate for a range of audiences and purposes.
Students will employ critical thinking to analyze forms of communication.
Students will engage in writing processes that involve drafting, revising, and reflecting.
components.title: Student Learning Outcomes

components.text:
In ENC 1101, students will learn:
To develop rhetorical knowledge for effective communication to a range of audiences and for various purposes.
To understand how knowledge of writing concepts and practices can be applied effectively across various writing situations.
To analyze, interpret, and convey conclusions about a range of texts and representations of meaning.
To engage in critical thinking and reflective practices that help develop analytical and problem-solving abilities and foster meta-cognition.
To compose in different genres using knowledge of concepts and practices of writing and drawing on analysis of other texts as examples of writing strategies appropriate to context.
To effectively communicate ideas and present information clearly and concisely across contexts, in written, oral, and digital forms.
To understand and engage in composing as a recursive process that involves drafting, revising, and reflecting across multiple iterations.

components.text:
Students will be evaluated on the knowledge and practices of writing they develop, on the drafts and final compositions produced, on specific course engagement activities, and on weekly collaborative work, readings, and a range of low-stakes writing-to-learn activities in class or assigned as homework.
Attending and engaging in class and with course work is important in the study of writing as the subject matter of this course. As a discussion-based course, this involves not just submitting assignments but learning about writing effectively and appropriately to each situation. Much of the learning is completed during class or engagement activity and cannot be replicated otherwise. Success in each project in this course depends greatly on attendance and engagement in class.
Online courses have similar expectations. Although students do not physically attend, they must engage with the course materials and collaborate with others in a sequence designed for engaged learning. This means staying on pace throughout the course and engaging in weekly discussions and activities that build toward subsequent weeks and projects.
This is not a self-paced course.

components.text:
Percentages for each project are listed below. All grades within the course are entered into Canvas. Mid-term and final grades are submitted to the registrar. While Canvas assignments are calculated in points, projects and course engagement are assigned a percentage of the final course grade as listed below.
Instructors provide formative, actionable feedback to students on selected assignments and drafts to help students move successfully between drafts to the final projects. Course Engagement activities are not designed for feedback but as a measure of learning, indicated by points earned.
Project grades reflect the final product submitted, with course engagement designed to build knowledge around each project as students develop them. Course engagement (learning activities, reading, responses, drafting and other process work, discussions, collaborative and individual exercises, peer review, reflection and writing-to-learn assignments, and all other related course work aside from project submissions) make up a specific percentage of the final grade (40%), as they are designed specifically to engage students in learning the subject matter of the course and to ensure the learning outcomes for the course are met.
Project 1: Rhetorical Analysis -- 15%
Project 2: Writing Contexts Presentation -- 15%
Project 3: Digital Composition -- 15%
Project 4: Final Analysis Essay -- 15%
Course Engagement -- 40% (as noted above, includes learning activities and discussions within class, reading responses, project drafts and process work, collaborative and individual exercises and activities, quizzes, peer reviews, reflection writing, and all other related course work aside from Project Submissions)
#GEA 1 – General Education Assessment Assignment
The Final Analysis Essay as listed above under Project 4 will assess student learning. In this project, students will write an essay both reflecting on and analyzing their knowledge about writing as they look back over their work in the course. Through a series of prompted reflection responses and drawing on their own work as evidence, students will theorize about and articulate the knowledge they have developed about rhetorical concepts, communicating responsibly, understanding information presented across contexts, for various audiences and purposes, and utilizing appropriate tools and rhetorical moves. In a clear and cohesive essay, students will analyze their writing knowledge and connect what they know to the writing they have studied that demonstrates understanding of rhetorical concepts across contexts, audiences, and purposes.
components.title: Grade Categories and Weights

components.text:
Feedback
Instructors provide formative, actionable feedback on writing assignments or drafts to help students move successfully through the sequenced learning of the semester. Course engagement activities vary in design and expected feedback; all provide a measure of learning and an opportunity for students to build their knowledge toward the development of each project.
Instructors will provide more substantial feedback on selected individual student work throughout the semester, such as project drafts. Feedback will be provided collectively on selected activities or project work. Students are responsible for revisions, using feedback, self-assessment activities, and reflection on knowledge and process to make rhetorical decisions about their own written work.
Instructors will provide feedback in a timely manner to allow students time to consider suggestions and make revisions to project work. Instructors provide feedback in Canvas, or via in-class presentation or Canvas Announcement for collective discussion.
Feedback is an important part of the writing process, and it is expected that students consider feedback carefully and ask questions as necessary regarding feedback received. Whether or not to incorporate feedback into writing or revision is ultimately the writer's decision.

components.text:
Florida Statute 1004.097 Free Expression on Campus
Students may, without prior notice, record video or audio of a class lecture for a class in which the student is enrolled for their own personal, educational use (USF Policy 10-048). A class lecture is defined as a formal or methodical oral presentation as part of a university course intended to present information or teach enrolled students about a particular subject. Recording class activities other than class lectures, including but not limited to lab sessions, student presentations (whether individually or part of a group), class discussion, clinical presentations such as patient history, academic exercises involving student participation, test or examination administrations, field trips, private conversations between students in the class or between a student and the faculty member is prohibited. Recordings may not be used as a substitute for class participation and class attendance and may not be published or shared without the written consent of the faculty member. Failure to adhere to these requirements may constitute a violation of the USF Student Conduct Code.

components.text:
Participation and Attendance
This is primarily a discussion-based, writing intensive course which requires attendance, collaboration, and engagement in class in order to learn. Therefore, 40% of the total course grade is allocated to course engagement in a variety of ways in every class meeting and weekly module. This engagement cannot be replicated or made up if class is missed. Students who miss classes, don't engage in course work, or have extended absence will miss out on the scaffolded design and learning required in this course, which will ultimately affect a student's ability to meet learning outcomes needed to pass the course and will impact final grade.
Students with university-excused absences should alert the instructor in advance. Participation and course engagement activities cannot be made up but may be excused for a university-approved absence.
Repeated late arrivals to class, early departures, or otherwise missing a significant portion of the class meeting, may result in no credit or minimal credit for course engagement in that class period, at the instructor’s discretion. Attendance and participation run from class start time to the end of class for each class meeting.
Attendance is taken. Attendance is expected at every class. Plan ahead for illness or emergency by attending all other class meetings so any necessary absences can be mitigated by having attended regularly the rest of the time. Missing a class does not excuse the student from the responsibility of assignments or due dates. Contact your instructor in advance to request additional time if necessary. Contact a classmate for any potential notes taken or consult Canvas for due dates or information.
First-Day Attendance Requirement
First-day attendance (FDA) is mandatory for all students per USF policy. Instructors are required to submit to the registrar any names of students absent for the first class. The registrar will drop students from the course for non-attendance on the first day of class (unless the student adds the course after that date).
Sometimes students experience extenuating circumstances and are unable to attend the initial class meeting. They must indicate intent to attend the class by notifying the instructor by email prior to the first meeting, and providing relevant documentation, so the instructor can count that student as present for first-day attendance purposes. Any student not in attendance and who has not been excused from attending the first class by their instructor, will be dropped from the course.
In online sections, students may be asked to complete an activity or assignment to satisfy the FDA requirement.
Class Disruption
Repeated tardiness, leaving and returning to class, early departure, use of cell phones or not silencing notifications, and other disruptive behaviors affect every student's learning experience. Such disruption will be addressed by the instructor and may result in an Academic Disruption Report filing.
Late Work
All course work should be submitted by its due date. Late work is generally not accepted. For students requiring accommodations related to on-time submission, please submit documentation to the instructor in advance.
Instructors, at their discretion, may offer reasonable extensions or move due dates on assignments for all students. Individual students may be granted extensions with or without penalty at the instructor's discretion for a limited time, based on extenuating circumstances.
Each major project builds on the last, therefore any extensions can only be permitted for a limited time, generally no more than a few days (at instructor’s discretion). Late work related to or within a project, cannot be submitted after that project is completed, and if an extension is provided. A project due date or extension date (if granted) is the last date a project, or any assignment affiliated with that project, can be submitted for a grade. Most course engagement work will be due during the class it is assigned and cannot be made up.
All due dates for course work are clearly indicated. Meeting those deadlines is a student’s responsibility as is communicating with the instructor in advance. If an extension for an assignment is requested, the student should do so prior to its due date by emailing the instructor.
Student Responsibility for Accurate Assignment Submission
Students are required to submit assignments by the due dates, which are provided well in advance. If an instructor changes a due date, the change will always extend, not shorten, the time allowed.
Some course due dates fall on weekend days to give students maximum time to work on them. This design allows students with weekday obligations to complete assignments on weekends. It also allows students with weekend obligations enough time to complete assignments and upload before the weekend if that's an individual's preference. It is the responsibility of students to manage their time according to their own commitments.
It is also the student's responsibility to ensure uploads to Canvas correspond to the correct assignment. This includes ensuring an assignment is uploaded correctly and is not a partial, unfinished, or incorrect draft, or the submission may be counted as no submission and earn a zero score. Students should check uploads for correct attachments and open the attachment to check for successful submission. If attempts to submit work are unsuccessful, students should rectify by submitting a Help Ticket to Canvas. If Help Desk assistance is ongoing but might go beyond deadline, contact your instructor. Please alert your instructor regarding any assignment submission concerns before that assignment is due.
Timely Grading
Instructors will endeavor to evaluate and assign grades to projects in a timely manner, usually within two weeks following the submission of a major project. Grades on smaller assignments will be provided continuously, but may be prioritized by significance to upcoming projects.
Extra Credit
There is no extra credit available in this course.
Examinations
While there are no exams in this course, the final project acts as a final exam of sorts as it represents the culmination of learning in the course and represents a significant portion of the final course grade.
Minimum Passing Grade Required: C- for general education credit

components.text:
The current university policy concerning incomplete grades will be followed in this course.
For undergraduate courses: An “I” grade may be awarded to a student only when a small portion of the student’s work is incomplete and only when the student is otherwise earning a passing grade. The time limit for removing the “I” is to be set by the instructor of the course. For undergraduate students, this time limit may not exceed two academic semesters, whether or not the student is in residence, and/or graduation, whichever comes first. For graduate students, this time limit may not exceed one academic semester. “I” grades not removed by the end of the time limit will be changed to “IF” or “IU,” whichever is appropriate.

components.text:
It is fundamental to the University of South Florida’s mission to support an environment where divergent ideas, theories, and philosophies can be openly exchanged and critically evaluated. Consistent with these principles, this course may involve discussion of ideas that you find uncomfortable, disagreeable, or even offensive.
In the instructional setting, ideas are intended to be presented in an objective manner and not as an endorsement of what you should personally believe. “Objective” means that the idea(s) presented can be tested by critical peer review and rigorous debate, and that the idea(s) is supported by credible research.
In this course you may be asked to engage with complex ideas and to demonstrate an understanding of the ideas. Understanding and engaging with an idea does not require you to believe it or to agree with it.

This course requires internet connection and access to Canvas as all course work is submitted to and communicated within the Canvas LMS. Lack of access to a computer is not an excuse for assignments that are not complete or not submitted on time.
If attempts to submit work are unsuccessful, students should seek assistance by submitting a Help Ticket to Canvas. If Help Desk assistance is ongoing but might go beyond deadline, contact your instructor. Please alert your instructor regarding any assignment submission concerns before that assignment is due.
For assistance with other technology, please contact USF IT or Canvas IT help desk as appropriate. Instructors cannot verify or assist with technology, only with the course content in Canvas. Students are responsible for addressing technical difficulties with the appropriate support provided by USF and may want to alert the instructor if a technological challenge affects their work in the course. On rare occasions in which technology across USF systems are affected (such as a weather event) the university and/or instructor will advise about how to proceed.
The following technologies will be used in this course. See also Student Expectations below:
Email: Students should check their USF email account and Canvas for messages or announcements daily. Emails with instructors should be conducted using your usf.edu account.
Canvas: Use of Canvas is required at USF. For assistance, use the Canvas Guide (Links to an external site) and/or contact Canvas help desk.
MS Teams: Your instructor may hold some office hours or conferences in Microsoft Teams (Links to an external site), or use Teams for individual student consultations.
Use of Generative AI: All students are expected to understand the ethical implications of GenAI use in this course and to disclose use of GenAI for any assignments where GenAI has been used when permitted. Acceptance of assignments using GenAI is up to the discretion of the instructor, and in this class that often depends on the parameters for each assignment. Please consult the detailed explanation of student responsibility and assignments in which GenAI use is permitted in this course as outlined below and consult the instructor to clarify expectations before submitting any work where GenAI was used.

components.text:
Health and Wellness
Your health is a priority at the University of South Florida. We encourage members of our community to look out for each other and to reach out for help if someone is in need. If you or someone you know is in distress, please make a referral at www.usf.edu/sos so that the Student Outreach & Support can contact and provide helpful resources to the student in distress. A 24-hour licensed mental healthcare professional, offered through the counseling center, is available by phone at 813-974-2831, option 3. Please remember that asking for help is a sign of strength. In case of emergency, please dial 9-1-1.
Title IX Policy
USF is committed to fostering a safe and respectful learning environment, free from sex discrimination and sexual harassment, in accordance with Title IX and USF Policy 0-004. If a student shares an experience of sexual harassment, sexual assault, stalking, or relationship violence with a USF employee (including faculty), that employee will notify the Title IX Office. This allows the Title IX Office to send the student an email with information about support resources and options—if it is safe to do so. Students are not required to respond to this email. The Title IX Office is a private resource. Information is shared only on a need-to-know basis to provide students with support measures. To speak to a confidential resource, students may contact USF Center for Victim Advocacy at 813-974-5757. Confidential resources do not notify the Title IX Office unless the student requests it. For more information about Title IX, available resources, or to make a report, please visit www.usf.edu/title-ix.
Discrimination / Harassment
Discrimination or harassment of students based on protected characteristics is prohibited by Title VI, the Florida Educational Equity Act, and USF Policy 0-007. Protected characteristics include race, color, national origin, shared ancestry, religion, age, sex, disability, genetic status, marital status, and veteran status. If a student shares an experience of harassment or discrimination with a USF employee (including faculty), that employee will notify the Student Equal Opportunity Office. This allows the Student EO Office to send the student an email with information about support resources and options—if it is safe to do so. Students are not required to respond to this email. The Student EO Office is a private resource. Information is shared only on a need-to-know basis to provide students with support measures. For more information about Student EO, available resources, or to make a report, please visit www.usf.edu/student-eo
Course Hero / Chegg Policy
The USF Policy on Academic Integrity specifies that students may not use websites that enable cheating, such as by uploading or downloading material for this purpose. This does apply specifically to Chegg.com and CourseHero.com – almost any use of these websites (including uploading proprietary materials) constitutes a violation of the academic integrity policy.
Professionalism Policy
Per university policy and classroom etiquette; mobile phones, iPods, etc. must be silenced during all classroom and lab lectures. Those not heeding this rule will be asked to leave the classroom/lab immediately so as to not disrupt the learning environment. Please arrive on time for all class meetings. Students who habitually disturb the class by talking, arriving late, etc., and have been warned may suffer a reduction in their final class grade.
Turnitin.com
In this course, turnitin.com may be utilized. Turnitin is an automated system which instructors may use to quickly and easily compare each student's assignment with billions of web sites, as well as an enormous database of student papers that grows with each submission. Accordingly, you may be expected to submit all assignments in both hard copy and electronic format. After the assignment is processed, as instructor I receive a report from turnitin.com that states if and how another author’s work was used in the assignment. For a more detailed look at this process visit http://www.turnitin.com.
Netiquette Guidelines
Act professionally in the way you communicate. Treat your instructors and peers with respect, the same way you would do in a face-to-face environment. Respect other people’s ideas and be constructive when explaining your views about points you may not agree with.
Be sensitive. Be respectful and sensitive when sharing your ideas and opinions. There will be people in your class with different linguistic backgrounds, political and religious beliefs or other general differences.
Proofread and check spelling. Doing this before sending an email or posting a thread on a discussion board will allow you to make sure your message is clear and thoughtful. Avoid the use of all capital letters, it can be perceived as if you are shouting, and it is more difficult to read.
Keep your communications focused and stay on topic. Complete your ideas before changing the subject. By keeping the message on focus you allow the readers to easily get your idea or answers they are looking for.
Be clear with your message. Avoid using humor or sarcasm. Since people can’t see your expressions or hear your tone of voice, meaning can be misinterpreted.
Email and Discussion Board Guidelines
Use the subject line effectively by using a meaningful line of what your email or discussion is about.
Keep your emails and postings related to the course content. You should not post anything personal on a discussion board unless it is requested by the instructor.
Any personal, course or confidential issues should be directly communicated to the instructor via email. The discussion boards are public spaces; therefore, any issues should not be posted there.
End of Semester Student Evaluations
All classes at USF make use of an online system for students to provide feedback to the University regarding the course. These surveys will be made available at the end of the semester, and the University will notify you by email when the response window opens. Your participation is highly encouraged and valued.
Food and Drink Policy (for in-campus sessions only).
Please adhere to the firm policy of no beverages (other than bottled/capped water), food, tobacco products, or like items in the classroom. Your understanding of the necessity for this policy and cooperation will be greatly appreciated. This policy will be strictly enforced.

The USF Office of Student Success coordinates and promotes university-wide efforts to enhance undergraduate and graduate student success. For a comprehensive list of academic support services available to all USF students, please visit the Office of Student Success website.
Canvas Technical Support
If you have technical difficulties in Canvas, you can find access to the Canvas guides and video resources in the “Canvas Help” page on the homepage of your Canvas course. You can also contact the help desk by calling 813-974-1222 in Tampa or emailing help@usf.edu.

Student Ombuds Office

Ombuds can help students safely explore options, clarify processes, and consider next steps. Learn more or make an appointment at usf.edu/student-ombuds.
